title: Categorical versus continuous perception

sides.name: Categorical perception
points: Labels switch sharply over a step or two of the continuum.
Discrimination peaks at the category boundary and is near chance inside a category.
Similarity is defined by linguistic category.
This is what Liberman and colleagues (1957) found.

sides.name: Continuous, non-categorical perception
points: Labels change gradually with distance from each prototype.
Discrimination is flat, the same for every equally spaced pair.
Similarity is defined by physical distance.
This is the ideal observer prediction that the data rejected.

why: The comparison explains why equal acoustic steps can sound very different. It also explains why categorical perception was treated as the step from physical to symbolic.

title: Thresholded versus cascaded processing

sides.name: Thresholded, the lumber mill
points: Activity passes forward only after a threshold is crossed.
Categorical perception arises at phoneme identification.
Every /b/ sends the same finished phoneme to the word level.
Competitor looks should not change with distance from the boundary.

sides.name: Cascaded, the food web
points: Activity passes forward continuously over time.
Categorical perception may arise later or be an artifact of the task.
A /b/ near the boundary also sends some support for /p/.
Competitor looks should rise as VOT nears the boundary, as McMurray and colleagues (2003) found.

why: The eye movement data favor the cascade, because graded competition appears even when the final click is the same.

title: Late correction versus boundary shift for the Ganong effect

sides.name: Late correction
points: Categorical perception works as usual, then a bias favors reporting a word.
The lexical effect is the same size at every step.
Word knowledge acts after perception.

sides.name: Boundary shift
points: Word knowledge moves the category boundary itself.
The lexical effect peaks near the boundary and is near zero at the endpoints.
Word knowledge acts during perception, through feedback in TRACE.

why: Ganong’s lexical effect peaked near the boundary, so the results fit the boundary shift account.

title: Autonomous syntactic parsing versus early interaction

sides.name: Autonomous syntactic parser
points: The parser uses only abstract syntactic structure.
It follows minimal attachment and late closure.
Garden paths come from fixed structural preferences.
Context can only repair the parse afterward.

sides.name: Early interaction
points: Meaning, word statistics and context work with syntax from the start.
Preferences depend on words, as with the burglar and the policeman.
Many reduced relatives are easy, so structure alone does not predict difficulty.
Context changes the first parse, as with one apple versus two.

why: Both views explain garden paths, but only early interaction explains why the same structure is sometimes easy and sometimes hard.

title: Broca’s aphasia versus Wernicke’s aphasia

sides.name: Broca’s aphasia
points: Telegraphic speech with word-finding pauses.
Grammatical morphemes and word order are disturbed, and content words are relatively spared.
Comprehension seems good in conversation but fails when syntax conflicts with common sense.
Described as a problem with grammar, and linked to anterior damage and production.

sides.name: Wernicke’s aphasia
points: Fluent speech with good intonation.
Word salad with neologisms, while syntax is roughly intact.
Comprehension is poor overall, even on simple sentences.
Described as a problem with activation in the lexicon, and linked to posterior damage and perception.

why: The split looked like a grammar and lexicon double dissociation. Later work with stressed listeners and nonverbal tasks weakened the claim that the deficits are purely linguistic.

title: Competence versus performance in Broca’s aphasia

sides.name: Competence account
points: Broca’s patients have lost grammatical knowledge.
Caramazza and Zurif (1976) found trouble when only syntax gives the answer.
The deficit should be specific to syntax.

sides.name: Performance account
points: Broca’s patients keep grammatical knowledge but lack resources to use it.
Stressed undergraduates showed the same trouble with object clefts and passives.
Saygin and colleagues (2004) found deficits in nonverbal action tasks too.

why: The same sentence pattern can come from lost knowledge or from reduced processing resources, so the healthy-listener data matter.

title: Nativist versus emergentist accounts of speech categories

sides.name: Nativist
points: Children have innate knowledge of what language is like.
Infants start as citizens of the world, able to hear all contrasts.
Learning only selects and narrows innate contrasts.
Categorical perception is special to language and to humans.

sides.name: Emergentist
points: Associative learning picks up statistical regularities in the input.
Some contrasts start hard and need exposure, as Narayan and colleagues (2010) found.
Learning builds categories from distributions, as Maye and colleagues (2002) found.
Categorical perception appears for non-speech and in chinchillas.

why: The findings that categorical perception is not limited to language or humans, and that some contrasts must be learned, favor learning within constraints.

title: Critical period versus sensitive period

sides.name: Critical period
points: Discrete, programmed onset and offset.
No learning before or after the window.
Any late improvement counts against it.

sides.name: Sensitive period
points: Gradual onset and offset that experience can shift.
Learning is possible throughout life but best during the window.
Late improvement is harder but possible, as with adult amblyopia training.

why: Amblyopia and most language evidence fit a sensitive period better, because late learning is reduced rather than impossible.

title: Exercise hypothesis versus maturational state hypothesis

sides.name: Exercise hypothesis
points: Early in life, humans have a superior capacity for acquiring languages.
The capacity declines only if it is not exercised.
An adult who learned an L1 normally should learn an L2 as well as a child.

sides.name: Maturational state hypothesis
points: Early in life, humans have a superior capacity for acquiring languages.
The capacity declines with maturation whether or not it is exercised.
An adult with a normal L1 should still learn an L2 less well.

why: Johnson and Newport’s learners all had a normal L1 yet later arrivals did worse, so the data fit the maturational state hypothesis. Only L2 data can separate the two.

title: Implicit versus explicit knowledge (Ellis, 2005)

sides.name: Implicit knowledge
points: Intuitive awareness of linguistic norms.
Procedural, knowing how.
Variable but systematic.
Reached through automatic processing.
Used in fluent performance.
Cannot be put into words.
Possibly learnable only within the critical period.

sides.name: Explicit knowledge
points: Conscious awareness of rules.
Declarative, knowing that.
Anomalous and inconsistent.
Reached through effortful controlled processing.
Used when planning or struggling.
Can be put into words.
Learnable at any age.

why: An untimed GJT allows explicit knowledge, so an age effect on it may not measure the implicit grammar the critical period is about.

title: Children versus adults learning a second language

sides.name: Children
points: Learn slowly at first, about 20 words by 18 months.
Build concepts and words together.
Often reach native-like ultimate attainment if they start early.

sides.name: Adults
points: Learn faster at first, through transfer and better general cognitive skills.
Already have concepts and focus on how the new language expresses them.
Rarely become native-like, partly because of transfer.

why: Speed of learning and ultimate attainment are separate measures, so children and adults each win on one of them.

title: Positive versus negative transfer

sides.name: Positive transfer
points: Cognates and loan words make new vocabulary easier.
De Groot and Keijzer (2000) found cognates learned faster and kept longer.
Typologically similar languages benefit more, as with Spanish speakers learning English.

sides.name: Negative transfer
points: One L1 category can hide an L2 contrast, as with Hindi dental and retroflex stops.
Classifiers and grammatical gender use cues English speakers learned to ignore.
False friends such as embarazado lead to errors.

why: The same habit of using L1 knowledge speeds learning where languages match and causes errors where they differ.

title: Listening in L2 versus listening in L1 (Marian and Spivey)

sides.name: Task in L2, English
points: Russian competitors drew looks about twice as often as a control.
L1 words are active during L2 listening.
Strong L1 conceptual links let a partly active Russian word activate its concept.

sides.name: Task in L1, Russian
points: English competitors did not reliably draw looks.
L2 words are not reliably active during L1 listening.
Weak L2 conceptual links cannot create this interference reliably.

why: The Revised Hierarchical Model explains the asymmetry through the difference in conceptual link strength between the two lexicons.
